title: Pre-swing big bands and saxophonists admired
summary: Pre-swing bands groping toward swing; Pat Davis and Hutchinrider are recalled.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: This is Rio 3, Henry Comin, February the 13th, 1963. We're talking about Saxe Mansfield. He was one you liked.

Yeah, I don't think I would like him today, but he played in the Eysom Jones band. These are all pre-swing bands, but there were a lot of bands that played big band jazz. That didn't come out with the swing era, nor you know it's often said that that problem was solved with Fletcher Henderson when he began to write the line. He may have perfected it, but there were a lot of bands groping your way toward trying to play some kind of big band jazz or swing music before. And many bands that might be primarily so-called sweet bands, usually at any dance, you played in sets, and it was pretty often that you're trying to get a slow number and a medium number, say, and possibly now and again a waltz. Not much Latin then. But you always ended the set with an up-tempo, and it had to swing in some way. After all, the Castle Oma band was trying to grope toward this, and before that it was the Gene Goldkamp band, the Castle Oma band.
Yeah, well, of course, if the people knew him beforehand, it never started arranging. That's what I believe, yes. Yeah, well, Don Redman was doing his arrangements for him before that.
But, uh, oh, and I don't know. Then there was a guy in the Castle Oma band, I think his name was Pat Sullivan? No, Pat… The Tenor Club?

Pat Davis. Pat Davis. Pat Davis. He was much admired by almost all the saxophone players I knew. In fact, some of them, at one time he used a baritone mouthpiece on a tenor to get a broader sound, and that became a thing a lot of guys did, put a baritone mouthpiece on a tenor. But very soon they came to regard him as nothing. He wasn't really a lasting man or a lasting influence. Whereas Hutchins Ryder, a clarinet player, was good then and has been good all the way, and sounds remarkably good today.
